questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gravitational Force Between Two Objects
questions.problem:
Earth has a mass of $(5.97\times {10}^{24})\,\text{kg}$ and the Moon has a mass of $(7.35\times {10}^{22})\,\text{kg}.$
The average distance between the centers of Earth and the Moon is $(3.84\times {10}^{8})\,\text{m}.$ According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, what is the magnitude of the gravitational force between Earth and the Moon? Write your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate. Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}).$

The magnitude of the force between Earth and the Moon is
$(${{field-1}}
$\times $
{{field-2}}$)\,\text{N}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\text{N}),$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

Let ${m}_{1}$ be the mass of Earth and ${m}_{2}$ be the mass of the Moon. Then, substituting in the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\cdot \frac{(5.97\times {10}^{24})\cdot (7.35\times {10}^{22})}{(3.84\times {10}^{8})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6.67\cdot 5.97\cdot 7.35}{(3.84)^{2}}\times \frac{{10}^{-11}\cdot {10}^{24}\cdot {10}^{22}}{({10}^{8})^{2}} \\  & =(19.848\,37…)\times {10}^{19} \\  & =(1.984\,837…)\times {10}^{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to three significant figures, the gravitational force between Earth and the Moon is
$(\,1.98\times {10}^{20}\,)\,\text{N}.$

Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}).$

The mass of the other object is

$\times $
{{field-2}}$)\,\text{kg}.$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ F{r}^{2} & =G{m}_{1}{m}_{2} \\ {m}_{2} & =\frac{F{r}^{2}}{G{m}_{1}}\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, rounded to two significant figures, the mass of the other object is
$(\,1.3\times {10}^{7}\,)\,\text{kg}.$

questions.problem:
The Sun has a mass of $(1.99\times {10}^{30})\,\text{kg}$ and Venus has a mass of $(4.87\times {10}^{24})\,\text{kg}.$ The magnitude of the gravitational force between them is $(5.54\times {10}^{22})\,\text{N}.$ According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, what is the distance between the centers of mass of the Sun and Venus? Write your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate. Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}).$

The distance between the Sun and Venus is
$(${{field-1}}
$\times $
{{field-2}}$)\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\text{N}),$

- $G=(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\,{\text{m}}^{3}/(\text{kg}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2})$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\text{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\text{m}.$

First, let's rearrange the formula to make $r$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ {r}^{2} & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F} \\ r & =\sqrt{G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{F}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${m}_{1}$ be the mass of the Sun and ${m}_{2}$ be the mass of Venus. Then, substituting in the known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\cdot \frac{(1.99\times {10}^{30})\cdot (4.87\times {10}^{24})}{5.54\times {10}^{22}} \\  & =\frac{6.67\cdot 1.99\cdot 4.87}{5.54}\times \frac{{10}^{-11}\cdot {10}^{30}\cdot {10}^{24}}{{10}^{22}} \\  & =(11.668…)\times {10}^{21} \\  & =(1.1668…)\times {10}^{22}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the square root, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{1.1668…\times {10}^{22}} \\  & =\sqrt{1.1668…}\times \sqrt{{10}^{22}} \\  & =(1.0801…)\times {10}^{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to three significant figures, the distance between the Sun and Venus is
$(\,1.08\times {10}^{11}\,)\,\text{m}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
The Sun has a mass of $(1.99\times10^{30})\,\textrm{kg}$ and Mars has a mass of $(6.42\times10^{23})\,\textrm{kg}.$
The average distance between the centers of the Sun and Mars is $(2.28\times10^{11})\,\textrm{m}.$ According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, what is the magnitude of the gravitational force between the Sun and Mars? Write your answer in scientific notation, rounding to **three significant figures** where appropriate. Assume the Newtonian constant of gravitation is $G = (6.67\times10^{-11})\,\textrm{m}^3/(\textrm{kg}\cdot\textrm{s}^2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force attracting two objects is proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers of mass:

$$
F = G\dfrac{m_1m_2}{r^2}
$$

where

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\textrm{N}),$

- $G = (6.67\times10^{-11})\,\textrm{m}^3/(\textrm{kg}\cdot\textrm{s}^2)$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\textrm{kg},$ and

- $r$ is the distance between their centers of mass, measured in $\textrm{m}.$

Let $m_1$ be the mass of the Sun and $m_2$ be the mass of Mars. Then, substituting in the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =(6.67\times {10}^{-11})\cdot \frac{(1.99\times {10}^{30})\cdot (6.42\times {10}^{23})}{(2.28\times {10}^{11})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6.67\cdot 1.99\cdot 6.42}{(2.28)^{2}}\times \frac{{10}^{-11}\cdot {10}^{30}\cdot {10}^{23}}{({10}^{11})^{2}} \\  & =(16.392\,5…)\times {10}^{20} \\  & =(1.639\,25…)\times {10}^{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounded to three significant figures, the gravitational force between the Sun and Mars is
$\Big(1.64 \times 10^{21}\Big) \,\textrm{N}.$

$$

- $F$ is the gravitational force between the objects, measured in Newtons $(\textrm{N}),$

- $G = (6.67\times10^{-11})\,\textrm{m}^3/(\textrm{kg}\cdot\textrm{s}^2)$ is the Newtonian constant of gravitation,

- $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the masses of the objects, measured in $\textrm{kg},$ and

First, let's rearrange the formula to make $m_2$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\ F{r}^{2} & =G{m}_{1}{m}_{2} \\ {m}_{2} & =\frac{F{r}^{2}}{G{m}_{1}}\end{aligned}
